Ganjang Pork Bulgogi

The soy fork of pork bulgogi: same thin slices, same fast tabletop grill, no gochujang in sight.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 01 / 20 meat recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant. The soy fork of pork bulgogi: same thin slices, same fast tabletop grill, no gochujang in sight. Ganjang bulgogi is the version for the table that wants the sweet-savory register without the heat — kids' approval guaranteed, adults' silence guaranteed, because it disappears first at every mixed grill. It is also the best introduction to the genre: everything you learn here (the thin slice, the single layer, the flip at the weep) transfers directly to the spicy cousin (#M13).

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • This marinade runs wetter than the spicy lane's — on purpose. The pear juice here is the sweet carrier, and the pan juice it makes over rice is half the dish. Whisk everything until the honey dissolves completely.
  • Marinate 2–4 hours, refrigerated. The pork's fat forgives the salt; lean loin would not — shoulder or collar, same rule as #M13.
  • While the grill heats: the rice bowl plan — juice is treasure here, so a domed pan or a pan with a rim catches what a straight grate would drop.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Medium-high fire, single loose layer, sixty to ninety seconds undisturbed. The wet marinade wants a hiss, not a roar — if it boils gray in its own liquid, the pan is crowded; lift half the batch off and do two rounds. Checkpoint — the slices take color at the edges while the marinade caramelizes on the pan behind them — the smell is sweet soy and pork fat, and the pan should be building a glossy brown film, not a watery boil.
  2. 02
    Flip at the beading edge, 60–90 seconds more, pull while the centers still shine. Scrape the pan's caramelized juice into a small bowl as you go — over rice is where it lands. Checkpoint — test piece: sweet-savory edge, juicy interior, no heat anywhere — the register should be round and gentle, with the pear as a perfume rather than a flavor.
  3. 03
    Platter, sesame over; the bowl route (rice, juice, slices) and the ssam route both open. Checkpoint — the rice bowl test: the juice should be glossy brown and spoonable, milder than the marinade tasted raw — if it is syrupy-sweet, pull the honey back a tablespoon next batch. Chef’s Note — this is the record to teach the genre on: no heat to manage, no paste to balance, and every technique signal visible — the weep at the edge, the single-layer law, the juice-vs-char trade. Cook it twice and you have earned the spicy fork (#M13); cook it four times and you will find yourself adjusting the garlic by smell, which is the table's graduation.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Slices boiled gray in marinadePan crowded or coolTwo smaller rounds; preheat fully
Syrupy, too sweetHoney over-run or slow panCut honey a tablespoon; hotter grate
Dry slicesLoin used or overcookedShoulder/collar; pull at shine
BlandUnder-marinated or light soyFull 2 hours; full-salt soy

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated pork keeps 24 hours. Cooked, 3 days — leftover ganjang bulgogi over cold rice with a fried egg and a spoon of the reserved juice is the lunchbox move.
  • Variations: the spicy fork (#M13); add gochugaru by the half-teaspoon to walk this lane toward the heat gently; chicken thigh takes the same marinade (#M16).
